title: ORDINANCE CHANGING THE BOUNDARIES OF THE CITY OF FLORIDA CITY, FLORIDA, AND AMENDING THE CHARTER OF SUCH MUNICIPALITY BY PROVIDING FOR THE ANNEXATION OF CERTAIN LANDS, UNDER AND PURSUANT TO PROCEEDINGS PRESCRIBED BY SECTION 5.04(B) OF THE HOME RULE CHARTER; PROVIDING FOR RESERVATION TO THE COUNTY OF ELECTRIC FRANCHISE, UTILITY TAX AND CIGARETTE TAX REVENUES; PROVIDING RETENTION OF GARBAGE AND REFU
report:
Chairman Martinez noted that although this was not a public hearing, he would allow Board members to make a statement on the record concerning the Mayoral veto of ordinance 05-111, changing the boundaries of the City of Florida City and providing annexation of certain lands, that was adopted by the BCC on 06/07/2005.
Commissioner Moss noted, for the record, that it was not the Board's intent to move the Urban Development Boundary (UDB) line as reported in the media, but to approve an ordinance annexing certain lands to Florida City. He noted Mayor Otis Wallace, Mayor of Florida City, had convinced him that the annexation would be beneficial to Florida City and that he agreed to remove the controversial areas that were considered wetlands. Commissioner Moss also noted testimony at the UDB workshop from the Army Corps of Engineers and the South Florida Management District that suggested there were no planned projects for the annexation area, and therefore no basis for claims that this annexation might jeopardize efforts to secure funding for the transit system.
It was then moved by Commissioner Moss that the Board override the Mayor's veto and allow this ordinance to become effective. This motion was seconded by Commissioner Jordan.

He noted the Board adopted a motion on January 16, 2014 to resolve the impasse for all eleven unions by eliminating the bargaining unit employee's five percent (5%) contribution and providing policy direction regarding the funding for the cost of such action. He advised that the motion adopted on January 16, 2014 was vetoed by Mayor Gimenez on January 24, 2014 and the veto appeared on today's agenda for the Board's consideration and possible override.
Mayor Gimenez presented his remarks on the five percent contribution of employees' base pay towards the County's healthcare costs and opined that eliminating this contribution was financially irresponsible; could jeopardize the County's ability to maintain their self-insurance program; could negatively impact the County's bond ratings; and would result in service reductions, vacant positions being eliminated and/or not filled, and employee layoffs.
Following Mayor Gimenez' presentation, Commissioner Jordan presented a motion to override the Mayor's veto on the motion adopted by the Board on January 16, 2014.

report:
County Attorney Abigail Price-Williams reported that Mayor Gimenez issued a veto on Resolution No. R-910-15 dated October 15, 2015, noting the Item was no longer in effect as a result of that veto. She said the Board could present a motion to adopt this resolution and become effective notwithstanding the Mayor's veto or the Mayor's veto would be deemed sustained.
Mayor Gimenez indicated that his opposition to this provision was presented at the October 6, 2015 County Commission meeting. He noted his veto message and comments from the Aviation Director addressed their concerns and asked the County Commission to sustain the veto.
In response to Commissioner Edmonson's and Chairman Monestime's requests for clarification, County Attorney Price-Williams explained that in order to override the veto, the motion would be to adopt Resolution No. R-910-15 and become effective notwithstanding the Mayor's veto. She noted a 'Yes' vote would be a vote to override of the veto.
Commissioner Zapata pointed out that he was the Resolution's sponsor and clarified that a 'Yes' vote would override the veto.
Hearing no further questions or comments, the Commission proceeded to vote on the forgoing proposed Mayoral Veto to override Resolution No. R-910-15.

title: ORDINANCE PERTAINING TO LEASES OF COUNTY PROPERTY FOR PRIVATE USE; AMENDING SECTION 2-8.9 OF THE CODE OF MIAMI-DADE COUNTY, FLORIDA; PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT OF LIVING WAGE TO CERTAIN HOURLY EMPLOYEES OF CERTAIN COUNTY LESSEES; PROVIDING EXCEPTIONS; PROVIDING SEVERABILITY, INCLUSION IN THE CODE, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE [SEE ORIGINAL ITEMS UNDER FILE NOS. 180300, 181054]
report:
County Attorney Abigail Price Williams read the foregoing Ordinance into the record. She noted the Mayor's veto and veto message were properly before the Board and the rules provide that this item shall be the first substantive item that this Board considers. The Mayor's veto stands unless two-thirds of the Commissioners present vote to override the veto.
With regards to his veto, Mayor Gimenez noted the long term consequences of requiring living wage for leases of County property for private use, particularly relating to the potential loss of jobs and revenue greatly outweigh any potential short term gains. He pointed out many contracts were not up for renewal until the year 2024 and the preliminary review by Regulatory and Economic Resources (RER) staff showed that this legislation would have a negative fiscal impact on many county projects and job opportunities associated with the projects. Mayor Gimenez explained that even Mom and Pop small businesses would be subject to paying living wages and this could hurt their small businesses; dozens of businesses would be affected and could cause a major impact, loss of jobs and revenue. He listed a number of businesses and projects that would be impacted due to this legislation, noting the potential job loss resulting from this legislation was 2,700 at a cost of $25 million.
